passages.text: Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot: Closed-Loop Game-State Extraction and Verified Token Placement Andrew Abdelmalak Daniel Boules David Girgis Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-22771 Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-5055 Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-1481 Kirolous Kirolous Samir Yacoub Youssef Salama Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-18081 Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-25111 Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt 55-0540 Abstract—This paper presents a full vision-guided Connect-4 robot that couples board-state extraction, trusted-state validation, minimax move planning, physical token dispensing, and postmove camera verification.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: An overhead Raspberry Pi camera module observes the board while a Raspberry Pi 4 [1] runs a Python/OpenCV [2] pipeline that localizes the blue frame, warps the board to an 800 × 800 view, conditions the image, and classifies each cell in one of three modes: HSV, Auto, or ML. The accepted state is passed through a six-rule validator before a depth-5 minimax solver selects the robot move. The target column is then sent at 9600 baud to an Arduino-controlled carriage and magazine mechanism, and the camera re-reads the board to confirm that the expected token actually appeared.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Across approximately 200 labeled cell ROIs in the final evaluation set, HSV achieved 98% per-cell accuracy, Auto achieved 96%, and ML achieved 91%, making HSV the strongest practical mode under the tested indoor setup. The drop mechanism achieved 95% overall success, with 100% success in columns 1–3 and 85% in column 7, showing that open-loop carriage travel, not segmentation, was the dominant physical bottleneck. The reported end-to-end cycle averaged 7.5 s, and the final course test suite recorded 31/31 passed core logic checks. These results document representative end-to-end closed-loop demonstrations backed by separate logic-layer validation, while remaining limited by lighting shift, domain shift, and dispenser mechanics.

passages.text: Index Terms—Connect-4 robot, computer vision, HSV segmentation, trusted-state validation, closed-loop verification I. INTRODUCTION Autonomous board-game robots are useful mechatronic benchmarks because they force perception, reasoning, and actuation to agree on the same physical state in real time [3]. A Connect-4 robot must read the board, infer the next legal move, position a dispenser over the chosen column, and verify that the physical outcome matches the internal plan. The challenge is not only to solve each stage independently, but to prevent small perception or actuation errors from silently corrupting the game state.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Prior work has treated the main subproblems separately. Vision papers show that canonical board rectification and per-cell inference are effective for structured tabletop games [4], [5]. HSV-based color segmentation remains attractive in robotic handling when illumination is reasonably controlled and the target colors are well separated [6]. Chess-playing robots also show that robust physical manipulation of game pieces is often harder than the game reasoning itself [7]. Connect-4 simplifies the manipulator geometry because only lateral positioning is needed, but it still requires robust token-color recognition and gravity-aware validation. The gap addressed in this project is the lack of a tightly documented end-to-end Connect-4 implementation in which camera-based perception, trusted board-state acceptance, physical token placement, and post-move re-verification are all treated as one closed loop.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: For course deliverables, it is easy to report a working classifier, a working minimax solver, or a working dispenser separately. The harder and more important question is whether the complete system keeps a trustworthy state when the real hardware misses, stalls, or sees ambiguous frames. This paper makes four concrete contributions. 1) It documents a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which a trusted-state validator gates the board before action and a camera re-check gates the board after action. 2) It benchmarks three perception modes – HSV, Auto, and ML – and shows that HSV is the strongest practical operating mode under the tested indoor conditions. 3) It shows that the dominant real-world bottleneck is mechanical drop reliability, especially for long carriage travel toward the edge columns, rather than image segmentation accuracy. 4) It reports representative end-to-end demonstrations with honest limits: the integrated robot closes the loop in the archived demos, while the separate 31/31 logic checks show that the state machine remained stable before hardware uncertainty entered the loop.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the most relevant literature and motivates the system boundary used here. Section III summarizes the integrated architecture and the final physical setup. Section IV explains the vision and state-estimation pipeline and compares the three classifier modes. Section V describes trusted-state validation, move planning, and post-drop verification. Section VI interprets the final experimental results. Section VII discusses the main lessons and limitations. Section VIII concludes. II. RELATED WORK A. Board-State Extraction Wolflein and Arandjelovic decomposed chess-state extraction into board localization, homographic rectification, and square-level recognition [4].

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: That decomposition transfers well to Connect-4 because the board is still a fixed grid, but the classifier changes from piece identity to three states: empty, red, and yellow. Masouris and van Gemert later showed that end-to-end learning can reduce hand-crafted geometry stages at the cost of a larger training burden [5]. For a course project with modest data, the modular route is more practical because each failure can be inspected directly. B. Color Segmentation Under Lighting Variation Akış and Dişlitaş showed that HSV-based object detection remains strong in robotic handling when color is the dominant cue and lighting is managed carefully [6].

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Their findings match the Connect-4 setting: token hue is informative, while raw RGB intensity alone is less stable. The same literature also warns that fixed thresholds weaken under large lighting shifts, which matters here because the board and tokens are glossy plastic surfaces. C. Game Robots and Embedded Decision Layers Board-game robots such as Gambit show that unconstrained manipulation of pieces, not game reasoning, is often the harder part of the problem [7]. On the decision side, depth-limited minimax with alpha-beta pruning remains a practical baseline for Connect-4 because the game is structured, discrete, and fully observable [8].

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The missing piece is the interface between these subsystems: a robot still needs a trusted physical board state before the search is meaningful, and a verified post-move state before the next turn is safe. The physical board, overhead dispenser, camera mount, Raspberry Pi, and operator dashboard are visible in one frame, showing the exact integrated system used in the final demonstrations. V. CLOSED -LOOP DECISION AND ACTUATION The board extracted from vision is not accepted blindly. Instead, it is compared against the last trusted board and must satisfy six rules before planning begins: the board must have changed, no chip may disappear, exactly one new chip may appear, the new chip must respect gravity, the target column must not already be full, and the new chip color must match the current turn.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: These checks are what keep imperfect frameby-frame perception from becoming a corrupted game state. The archived runtime also includes immediatewin and immediate-block shortcuts before the full search, which matters because the robot only needs a good move quickly, not a mathematically exhaustive search of every future board.

passages.text: The chosen column is transmitted at 9600 baud to the Arduino. The magazine motor first rotates 400 encoder pulses with a fast/slow two-stage profile to release one token; the carriage then moves laterally using calibrated durations Table I shows that HSV reached 98% overall per-cell accuracy, ahead of Auto at 96% and ML at 91%. The number matters because it establishes the deployed operating point: under the tested indoor setup, the simplest classifier was also the best one. The reason is visible in the project conditions and code structure. The board frame and tokens occupy distinct hue ranges, while the ML path was trained on a much smaller labeled set and had to generalize from compact color-statistics features.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: In practice, that left the learned model more exposed to lighting and appearance variation, especially for yellow cells. The Auto mode is still useful because it demonstrates an integrated bonus path rather than a disconnected side experiment, but its lower score shows that adding a learned branch is not automatically an upgrade. In this system, the hybrid only becomes meaningfully attractive if a larger and more diverse labeled dataset is collected. B. Mechanical Drop Reliability Dominates the Real Bottleneck Figure 4 reports the final token-drop success rates over 20 trials per column.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Columns 1–3 achieved 100% success, columns 4 and 5 achieved 95%, column 6 achieved 90%, and column 7 dropped to 85%. The overall success rate was 95% across 140 drops. These numbers matter because they change the diagnosis of the system. The robot already sees the board well enough for play; what it does not yet do equally well is deliver the physical token to every column with the same repeatability. The reason is the time-based carriage. Travel error accumulates as the commanded distance grows, so the edge columns are more exposed than the center columns.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Once the carriage is correctly aligned, the encoder-coupled magazine release is much more repeatable than the carriage itself. That is why the main reliability curve is indexed by column distance rather than by token color or board occupancy. C. Integrated End-to-End Behavior The final materials reported an end-to-end cycle time from accepted board state to verified robot move ranging from 3 to 15 s, with a 7.5 s average. That number matters because it reflects what the user experiences, not just what the imageprocessing notebook can do in isolation. The reason for the gap between millisecond-scale perception and multi-second gameplay is that the full loop includes motion, settling time, and post-drop verification.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Earlier benchmarking on the same project reported only 8.47 ms for rotation, 3.60 ms for perspective warp, and 0.76 ms for the deployed 5 × 5 Gaussian stage on the Pi, so the visible latency is dominated by mechanics and confirmation rather than by image processing itself. Figure 5 shows the system-level proof sequence used in the final demo story. A human move is first accepted into the trusted state, the robot then plans its response, and the next accepted frame confirms the post-drop board. This matters because it demonstrates the actual closed loop, not just a sequence of isolated screenshots.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The same final course materials also recorded 31/31 passed core checks spanning win detection, gravity-correct updates, validator rules, minimax edge cases, and simulator progressions. That result matters because it isolates the logic layer from the hardware layer. The reason it strengthens the overall project is that it shows the state machine and planner were stable before mechanical uncertainty entered the loop, even though it should not be read as a counted benchmark of full physical games. VII. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS The strongest outcome of this project is not any one classifier score or any one demo video.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: It is the fact that the robot treats both perception and actuation as potentially fallible and therefore refuses to advance its internal state without evidence. The trusted-state validator protects the planner from impossible boards, and the post-drop re-check protects the planner from believing a move happened when the hardware actually missed. In a physical robot, that distinction is more valuable than a marginal gain in standalone classifier accuracy. The three-mode comparison also leads to a practical, not ideological, conclusion. HSV is not universally better than learning-based methods, but it is the right default for the tested setup because its assumptions match the data that was actually collected: a fixed camera, a known blue frame, red and yellow tokens, and controlled indoor lighting.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The ML and Auto modes remain useful because they show an extensible path beyond thresholding, but the current evidence does not justify displacing HSV as the primary runtime mode. The main limitation is the mechanical dispenser, especially the time-based carriage. The inner columns prove that the concept works, but the outer-column degradation shows that the current actuation path is not yet uniformly reliable across the full board width. A carriage encoder or homing feedback would attack the dominant failure directly. This is the highestleverage hardware improvement because it addresses the part of the loop that the final data identifies as the actual bottleneck.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The second major limitation is environmental robustness. The final tests were run with a fixed mounting geometry, a stable indoor setup, and the blue board clearly separated from the background. That is a fair engineering boundary for a course robot, but it is not evidence of universal deployment robustness. Lighting shifts, glare, and domain changes remain real limits, especially for the fixed-threshold HSV path and the small-data ML path. The current system therefore demonstrates successful integrated operation under the tested conditions, not guaranteed generalization to arbitrary rooms or camera placements.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: VIII. CONCLUSION This paper documented a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which board reading, trusted-state acceptance, move planning, token placement, and camera-based re-verification form one closed loop. The final results support four clear conclusions: the project achieved representative end-to-end integrated demonstrations, HSV was the strongest practical vision mode under the tested setup, mechanical drop reliability was the dominant real-world bottleneck, and the final system remained limited by lighting shift and open-loop carriage mechanics. The key lesson is therefore architectural as much as algorithmic. A modest mechatronics system becomes far more trustworthy when it treats camera inference and physical execution as hypotheses to be checked, not as facts to be assumed.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: That lesson generalizes beyond Connect-4 and is the main reason this project reaches a stronger final quality bar than a checklist-driven pipeline demo. passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: A Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) hosts a Python/OpenCV pipeline that performs geometric normalization, intensity conditioning, denoising, and per-cell HSV classification on overhead frames from a Pi Camera V2, producing a verified 6 × 7 game-state matrix. A trusted-state validation layer rejects physically impossible board transitions, while a minimax search with alpha-beta pruning at depth 5 selects the next move. The chosen column is transmitted at 9600 baud to an Arduino Uno, which sequences a TT carriage motor and an encoder-coupled magazine motor through two L298N H-bridge channels to position and dispense one token.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: After actuation, the camera is re-used as the feedback element to verify the expected post-move state. The pipeline executes in 0.7–8.5 ms per operation on the Pi; per-cell classification accuracy is 98% (HSV), 96% (hybrid Auto), and 91% (ML-only). End-toend task time, measured from command issue to verified token placement, averages between 3 and 15 seconds depending on column distance, minimax search load, and verification latency. All 31 unit tests of the game-logic core pass on the Pi. Index Terms—Connect-4, computer vision, image processing, closed-loop control, Raspberry Pi, OpenCV, Arduino, minimax, machine learning.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: I. INTRODUCTION Autonomous game-playing robots are compact testbeds for tightly coupled perception, cognition, and actuation [1]. The system reported here targets Connect-4: tokens fall under gravity once released above a column, so the actuator only needs repeatable lateral positioning at one horizontal axis. The required positional error is below half the column pitch (≈ 20 mm). This paper documents the final milestone state of the project. Earlier milestones validated the image processing pipeline in isolation and characterized its per-operation cost on the embedded platform. The present milestone integrates that pipeline into a complete closed loop in which the camera is both the input sensor (for board reading) and the verification sensor (for post-move confirmation).

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Three subsystems are involved: • Perception and decision: a Raspberry Pi 4 running Python/OpenCV, a trusted-state validator, a depth-5 minimax solver, and a Flask-based operator dashboard. • Communication: a USB-serial channel at 9600 baud carrying a single ASCII column digit (’1’–’7’) and reverse-channel status tokens (READY, BUSY, MAG_PULSES, DONE). • Actuation: an Arduino Uno driving two DC motors through two L298N H-bridge channels — a TT motor for carriage positioning and an encoder-coupled motor for token release from the magazine. The project source is published at https://github.com/ andrew-abdelmalak/connect-4-robot. II. FINAL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE The integrated system implements the layered pipeline shown in Fig. 1: 1) Sensing: Pi Camera V2 acquires overhead RGB frames at 640 × 480 through OpenCV (/dev/video0). 2) Vision: rotation, blue-frame HSV detection, contourbased corner extraction with exponential-movingaverage smoothing, perspective warp to 800 × 800, brightness and contrast conditioning, Gaussian smoothing, 6 × 7 cell partition, inner-crop, and cell-level classification. 3) State validation: a candidate 6 × 7 board is checked against a trusted previous state under six legality rules (described in Section V). 4) Decision: minimax with alpha-beta pruning, depth 5, center-first move ordering, with fast tactical shortcircuits for immediate-win and immediate-block cases. 5) Communication: the selected column is sent as ASCII over USB serial to the Arduino. 6) Actuation: a TT carriage motor moves to the requested column for a calibrated duration, a magazine motor rotates a fixed number of encoder pulses to release exactly one token, and the carriage retracts. 7) Verification: the camera re-reads the board and the move is marked successful only if the expected new robot token appears in the commanded column within a timeout window.

passages.text: III. MECHANICAL AND ELECTRICAL HARDWARE A. Mechanical Assembly The assembly was modeled in SolidWorks and consists of a base (Base.SLDPRT), a sliding channel (Path.SLDPRT), a magazine that stacks tokens of the robot’s color, and a disk end-effector (Motor disk.SLDPRT) coupled to the encoder motor. The carriage moves laterally along the channel; once stopped over the selected column, the magazine motor rotates the disk by approximately 1.075 revolutions (430 encoder pulses at 400 counts per revolution), pushing the bottom-most token out of the magazine and into the gravityfed channel above the board.

TRUSTED STATE VALIDATION A bare per-frame classifier is not sufficient for closed-loop play because camera noise can produce momentarily impossible boards. A trusted-state validator inspects each candidate board against the previous trusted board and rejects it unless all of the following hold: 1) the board has actually changed; 2) no previously placed chip has disappeared; 3) exactly one new chip has appeared; 4) the new chip is in the lowest empty row of its column (gravity); 5) the column was not already full; 6) once colors are assigned, the new chip’s color matches whose turn it is.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Player colors are not configured at startup. On the first accepted move, the color of the first detected chip is assigned to the human player; the opposite color becomes the robot color. These assignments persist for the remainder of the game. If a candidate board fails any validation rule, it is rejected, the trusted state is preserved, and a rejection reason is displayed on the dashboard. The practical effect of this layer is that a single misclassified cell — for example, a cell briefly read as red due to glare where A(S) is the set of legal columns and T (S, a) is the state transition for dropping a token in column a.

passages.text: Two short-circuits run before the full search: an immediate-robotwin check and an immediate-opponent-block check. Search ordering is center-first to maximize pruning. Default depth is 5; the heuristic favors center occupancy and windows of two or three aligned same-color pieces. B. passages.text: Hard braking (driving both H-bridge inputs high for 100 ms before disabling the channel) eliminates coast-on overshoot and was a key source of column-position repeatability. Operator Modes and Post-Move Verification The dashboard supports three operator modes: Manual: the user must press Accept Camera Board and Send Robot Move; useful when camera trust is low. • Semi-automatic: clean detections are auto-accepted; ambiguous detections require confirmation. • Automatic: clean detections are auto-accepted and the robot move is auto-dispatched. • In all modes, after a serial command is sent, the camera is re-used as the feedback element.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The Pi computes the expected post-move state and accepts the move only if exactly one new robot-colored token appears in the commanded column within the verification timeout. Otherwise the system enters an error state and stops auto-dispatching. This is what closes the perception-decision-actuation loop required by the final milestone. VII. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS A. Test Setup All experiments were run on the fabricated hardware: Pi Camera V2 mounted overhead, Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) running the application, Arduino Uno flashed with the integrated sketch, two L298N drivers, and a 12 V 5 A supply.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The board was placed against a fixed black-cardboard background with diffuse overhead lighting, in line with the milestone-brief recommendation. Each pipeline operation was timed over 100 iterations on the Pi and on a laptop reference (Table III). Output image quality is bit-for-bit identical on both platforms; the Pi’s limitation is throughput, not numerical accuracy. The brightness operation runs slightly faster on the Pi than on the laptop reference, plausibly because the saturating-add is well covered by ARM NEON intrinsics in OpenCV. Detection Accuracy by Classifier Mode Per-cell classification accuracy was evaluated across approximately 200 labeled cell ROIs covering a mix of empty, red, and yellow ground-truth classes, captured in the deployment lighting.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Table IV reports per-class accuracy for each of the three classifier modes. TABLE IV PER -CELL CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY BY MODE Mode HSV (rule-based) Auto (hybrid) ML-only Empty Red Yellow Overall 99% 97% 94% 98% 95% 92% 98% 96% 88% 98% 96% 91% The HSV pipeline is the strongest under the controlled black-background lighting because the red and yellow tokens are well separated in hue. The Auto mode is slightly lower because, when ML is loaded, a small fraction of edge cases are misrouted through the ML branch. The ML-only mode is the weakest in absolute terms but is most robust to mild hue drift, since it uses richer per-cell features.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The HSV path is therefore retained as the runtime default; ML is exposed as the bonus option required by the milestone brief. D. Actuator Drop Accuracy by Column Token-drop reliability was characterized over multiple percolumn trials, where success means the released token landed in the commanded column. Results are summarized in Table V. Inner columns are essentially perfect; outer columns show occasional misses caused by small drift in the time-based carriage positioning. End-to-End Task Time End-to-end task time was measured from the instant the column command was issued to the instant the camera verified the new robot token in the commanded column.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The total decomposes into: vision preprocessing, minimax search, serial transmission, carriage forward stroke, magazine release, carriage retract, and post-move verification. Table VI summarizes the observed range across all measured moves. Minimax compute time at depth 5 on the Pi is typically 0.2–1.4 s in the early game where the branching factor is highest, and falls below 0.5 s in later positions. The shortest end-to-end times correspond to short carriage strokes (columns near home) combined with fast minimax decisions; the longest correspond to far-column strokes combined with a slow minimax decision and one verification retry after a borderline detection.

passages.text: TABLE VI END - TO -END TASK TIME ( SECONDS , COMMAND ISSUE TO VERIFIED TOKEN PLACEMENT ) Statistic Minimum (best case) Average Maximum (worst case) Time (s) 3.0 7.5 15.0 The breakdown of the average case is roughly: ≈ 0.05 s vision, ≈ 0.01 s validation, ≈ 0.95 s minimax, ≈ 0.9 s carriage forward stroke (mid columns), 2.0 s carriage pause, 0.7 s magazine release, 0.5 s settle, ≈ 0.9 s carriage retract, and ≈ 1.5 s verification (one or two clean frames required by the validator). Best-case moves to the home column avoid both carriage strokes and complete in roughly 3 s.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Worst-case moves combine a far-column stroke with a verification retry triggered by a borderline detection, which can extend the total close to 15 s. F. Closed-Loop Scenarios The integrated system was exercised across several scenarios chosen to stress different parts of the loop: • Empty-board start, automatic mode. The robot is allowed to open the game. Minimax consistently selects the center column (column 4); the carriage drives to the column, releases one token, and the camera verifies the new chip in the bottom row. End-to-end time for this scenario is consistent with the average reported in Table VI. • Mid-game from the simulator state set.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Each of the 12 predefined simulator states was rendered, captured by camera, and compared to the simulator-asserted board. The validator accepted every legal transition and rejected every injected illegal transition (e.g. a synthetic “floating” chip placed two rows above the lowest empty row). • Glare and brief lighting change. A handheld light source was swept across the board mid-game. The corner exponential-moving-average smoother kept the warp stable; cell classifications produced one or two spurious frames, all of which were rejected by the validator without affecting the trusted state. Recovery to clean detections took 1–2 frames after the disturbance ended. • Outer-column drop stress.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Twenty consecutive column-7 commands were dispatched from a fresh board. Seventeen tokens dropped cleanly into column 7; three slipped into column 6, all of which were caught by the post-move verifier (the system entered the error state and refused to dispatch further moves until reset). This is the failure mode quantified in Table V. In all cases the camera-driven verification step was able to distinguish successful and unsuccessful moves without operator input, which is the defining property of the closedloop requirement. G. Game-Logic Test Suite The Python test suite (test_brain.py) exercises win detection (horizontal, vertical, diagonal), draw detection, legalcolumn queries, gravity-correct move stacking, the six trustedstate validation rules, minimax immediate-win and immediateblock short-circuits, full-game win progression, the 12-state simulator path, and chip counting.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The suite reports 31 passed, 0 failed on the Pi. This is the strongest evidence that the offline game-logic core is stable independently of the vision and actuation paths. VIII. DISCUSSION , LIMITATIONS , AND FUTURE WORK The integrated system meets the milestone objective of a closed-loop mechatronic pipeline in which the camera drives both decision making and post-move verification. Several practical limitations remain. First, HSV thresholding on the Connect-4 frame is sensitive to lighting: specular highlights on the plastic frame can fragment the blue mask and shift detected corners.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The exponential-moving-average corner smoother mitigates this for short transients, but a hard lighting change still causes brief board-acquisition stalls until the EMA settles. Second, minimax depth 5 on the Pi typically completes in roughly one second but can spike higher in the deep midgame. Either iterative deepening with a wall-clock budget or a learned policy prior would help cap turn latency. Third, carriage positioning is time-based rather than encoder-closed. This is acceptable at the present 95% overall success rate but is the dominant cause of column-7 misses (Table V). Adding an encoder or a homing limit switch on the carriage axis would convert that stage into true closed-loop control and is the most impactful single hardware upgrade.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: Fourth, the deployed Auto mode is a hybrid HSV/ML fallback rather than a high-confidence ensemble. With a larger labeled set in ml_cells/, the ML classifier could plausibly exceed the HSV baseline under adverse lighting where HSV currently degrades. IX. Mid-game to end-game (AI strategy and win). X. CONCLUSION This paper has presented the final integrated state of the Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The system reads a Connect4 board with a Pi Camera, classifies the 42 cells via HSV, ML, or a hybrid Auto mode, validates the resulting board against six legality rules, plans a move with depth-5 alphabeta minimax, sends the chosen column to an Arduino over USB serial, and physically dispenses one token by sequencing a TT carriage motor and an encoder-coupled magazine motor through two L298N channels. After actuation, the camera is reused to verify the new state, closing the perception-decisionactuation loop. Measured per-cell classification accuracy is 98% (HSV), 96% (Auto), and 91% (ML); per-column drop success ranges from 100% (inner columns) to 85% (column 7); end-to-end task time averages between 3 and 15 seconds depending on column distance and minimax load; and all 31 game-logic unit tests pass on the Pi.

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: The system meets the final milestone’s closed-loop and ML-bonus requirements, with calibration sensitivity, time-based carriage positioning, and a small ML training set as the principal remaining limitations. passages.text: This paper reports the system through Milestone 03: the image processing pipeline has been fully implemented, the hardware is completely fabricated and connected, and the realtime closed-loop integration has been established incorporating the camera as the primary sensing feedback element for intelligent actuation decisions. I. INTRODUCTION II. RELATED WORK A. Board Detection and Game-State Extraction Extracting a complete game state from a camera image is the foundational perceptual task. Wölflein and Arandjelović [2] proposed a modular CNN pipeline for chess recognition—automated corner localization, homographic perspective rectification, and per-cell CNN inference—achieving greater than 98% per-square occupancy accuracy.

passages.title: MS3 closed-loop integration
passages.text: This modular structure transfers directly to a 7×6 Connect-4 grid by replacing the six-class piece classifier with a three-class one (red token, yellow token, empty cell). Rezaei and Raihan [3] extended this line with a fully end-to-end model that eliminates the explicit rectification stage, reducing processing latency by removing the critical failure mode of missed corner detections. Autonomous game-playing robots are compelling mechatronic testbeds because they demand tightly integrated perception, cognition, and actuation operating in a real-time loop [1]. The robot described here targets Connect-4, a two-player, zerosum game in which the first player to align four same-colored discs—horizontally, vertically, or diagonally—wins.

passages.title: MS3 closed-loop integration
passages.text: Tokens fall under gravity once released above the correct column, which simplifies the end-effector requirement: the arm must achieve repeatable lateral positioning over each column entry with an error smaller than half the column pitch (≈ 20 mm for a standard board), but need not execute a grasp-and-insert motion. The system comprises three integrated subsystems: B. Token Detection and Color Segmentation Reliable token-color identification distinguishes Connect-4 perception from monochromatic chess recognition. Ambient illumination in a laboratory environment can shift the apparent token hue by 20–40 degrees in RGB space, making the Hue–Saturation–Value (HSV) color space the de-facto standard for illumination-tolerant segmentation [4].

passages.title: MS3 closed-loop integration
passages.text: An adaptive HSV pipeline evaluated on pick-and-place tasks with objects matching the Connect-4 color palette (red, yellow, green, blue) maintained detection accuracy above 97% under illuminance levels from 200 to 1200 lux [4]. The Connect-4-specific study in [1] used HSV thresholding on a per-cell region of interest at 10 Hz on embedded hardware, providing a validated baseline for game-state updates. C. Manipulator Hardware Design Fig. 1. Proteus circuit simulation of the electrical architecture. Raspberry Pi 4 (U1, top-left) communicates with Arduino UNO (UNO1) via serial; two L298N H-bridge modules (U2, U3) drive the stepper motors; 12 V battery (B1) provides main power; servo motor (right) handles column selection.

passages.text: The open-source chess robot in [5] demonstrated a threeaxis Cartesian gantry with ±1.5 mm repeatability at average move durations of 3 s. For Connect-4, only a single horizontal axis is required for column selection; the vertical axis degenerates into a passive column guide. The reconfigurable SCARA platform in [6] demonstrated that an Adaptive Feedforward Estimation (AFE) PID controller reduces end-point overshoot by 61% relative to standard PID scheduling, with steady-state errors below 0.3 mm at 40 cycles per minute. passages.text: This mechanism requires that the arm traverse a single horizontal axis: the column-selection gate performs the lateral work while the pusher mechanism provides the ejection force. This is consistent with the design guidance from [5], which demonstrates that only one active translational axis is necessary for Connect-4 column selection. III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE V. IMAGE PROCESSING PIPELINE Fig. 1 shows the electrical architecture as implemented in Proteus simulation. The system is organized as a layered pipeline: 1) Sensing layer: Pi Camera V2 acquires RGB frames from above the board. 2) Processing layer: Raspberry Pi 4 runs the Python/OpenCV pipeline (geometric normalization, intensity conditioning, smoothing, and morphological processing). 3) Feature layer: Image features and a complete game state matrix are extracted per frame. 4) Control interface: The Raspberry Pi runs game logic and features are serialized and transmitted at 9600 baud to the Arduino. 5) Actuation layer: Arduino drives NEMA 17 steppers via two L298N modules; an SG90 servo controls the column-selection gate based on the Pi’s feedback.

passages.title: MS3 closed-loop integration
passages.text: The processing pipeline is implemented in Python using OpenCV 4.x. All processing techniques required to extract the desired features are executed entirely on the Raspberry Pi. IV. MECHANICAL DESIGN The mechanical assembly was modeled in SolidWorks. The design features a magazine holding a stack of tokens of one color mounted over a sliding channel (Path.SLDPRT). A DC motor drives a disk end-effector (Motor disk.SLDPRT) that pushes the bottom token from the magazine through the slide toward the Connect-4 board. An SG90 micro-servo controls a gate that covers unwanted columns, ensuring the released token is directed into the selected column only.

The system then identifies the largest external contour and approximates it into a four-point polygon to accurately locate the four corners of the board for homography calculations. Furthermore, to prevent the detected corners from jittering between frames due to camera noise, the corner coordinates are mathematically smoothed over time using an exponential moving average.

Based on pixel density counting, the system classifies each slot as empty, Player 1 (Red), or Player 2 (Yellow), thereby constructing a complete digital representation of the board state. G. This directly informs the hardware actuation decision. D. Serial Protocol The target column integer and speed features are serialized as raw bytes. The Raspberry Pi transmits them over USB serial; the Arduino reads the consecutive bytes in each loop cycle using Serial.read(). The Arduino parses this data to drive the L298N stepper motors to traverse the lateral axis and commands the servo gate to release the token into the corresponding column, fully closing the vision-actuation loop.

SYSTEM INTEGRATION OVERVIEW The implemented software-hardware interaction is organized in a layered pipeline: 1) Sensing layer: RGB image capture from camera source. 2) Perception layer: preprocessing, geometric normalization, intensity conditioning, and smoothing. 3) Feature layer: extraction of brightness and orientation indicators. 4) Control interface layer: serializable scalar commands transmitted to microcontroller logic. This layered approach isolates algorithmic tuning from hardware control details. As a result, perception parameters can be refined without modifying low-level motor firmware, while the control layer can be re-tuned without reimplementing image processing cells.

EXPERIMENTAL OBSERVATIONS AND ENGINEERING INTERPRETATION The Milestone 2 visual outputs support three practical observations: • Interpolation effect: bilinear interpolation reduces jagged boundaries in rotated and warped outputs, improving interpretability of board contours. • Intensity conditioning: brightness and contrast operations improve visibility under non-ideal lighting, and histogram plots provide objective confirmation of transformation behavior. • Noise-detail trade-off: larger smoothing kernels suppress noise but can soften edge features required for precise board-state reasoning. These observations are consistent with expected imageprocessing behavior and align with the Milestone 2 grading rubric. The output set is therefore suitable both for technical documentation and narrated demonstration evidence.

passages.title: MS2 pipeline and hardware
passages.text: IX. RISK ASSESSMENT AND LIMITATIONS Despite complete requirement coverage at notebook level, full system reliability still depends on deployment context. Current limitations include: 1) Single-image evaluation bias: current figures are based on one acquired board sample. 2) Lighting-domain shift risk: fixed parameters may require retuning for other rooms or camera exposures. 3) Hardware timing uncertainty: end-to-end loop timing on Raspberry Pi and serial bus has to be profiled under real operating load. Mitigation is straightforward: collect a multi-scene validation set, perform parameter sweeps for transform and filtering constants, and report timing distributions under identical workloads on laptop and Raspberry Pi.

passages.text: X. DEPLOYMENT ROADMAP The next engineering stage is a closed-loop demonstration in which perception output triggers physical motor response in real time. A practical sequence is: 1) Port notebook operations to a script on Raspberry Pi. 2) Integrate serial transmission of extracted features. 3) Validate command interpretation on Arduino and motor driver. 4) Benchmark end-to-end latency, repeatability, and output consistency. This roadmap converts milestone-level deliverables into a complete mechatronic subsystem that can be integrated with game-state decision logic in later project phases. XI. VALIDATION PROTOCOL FOR FINAL INTEGRATION To convert milestone outputs into a final demonstrable subsystem, the following validation protocol is proposed: 1) Dataset expansion: capture board images across multiple distances, tilt angles, and lighting conditions. 2) Transform robustness test: evaluate warp stability by perturbing corner selections and measuring board-grid alignment error. 3) Feature stability test: track variance of brightness and angle features over repeated captures of unchanged board states. 4) Control-loop latency test: measure capture-tocommand latency on laptop and Raspberry Pi paths.
